Should I pursue a linux based OS?

Over Windows, definitely. In general, it's a solid choice despite the future of the kernel becoming a bit uncertain now, though if you insist on your deployment being definitely free of faggotry then you have a few options:

  • Get a distro build from a year ago and/or use the terminal command uname -r to check the kernel version. Typically that can be done prior to the actual installation since most good distros can boot a live working/preview desktop from the image on a USB stick.
  • Install any distro build, then get the sources for an appropriate kernel version and make/install that to replace the kernel (may break a few things).

If so, what is a good linux OS for such a server?

Link: DistroWatch

  • Debian/Ubuntu types are quite widespread with good software package support. Most VPS services will default to Ubuntu Server, though note that this would be command-line only, whereas you may want a desktop GUI available.
  • CentOS is designed with servers in mind for extreme stability. It only uses software packages which are tested for a long amount of time.
  • Arch/Manjaro types have seen a recent surge in popularity, at least on the desktop rather than as a server.

Personally I use Linux Mint MATE edition for desktops (Mint is a Debian/Ubuntu type), and Ubuntu Server on my servers.

Should I consider a separate server for each site, or can I get away with hosting them all on one machine?

  • If it is purely HTTP services then you can definitely host them all on one box, even without using OS virtualization, since both Apache and Nginx support virtual hosts (speaking of that, I am a long-time Apache user since prior to the release of Nginx so I default to Apache, though I have deployed both).
  • Without OS virtualization, if you want other services as well then it depends on the services - for example, e-mail is notoriously complex to the extent that hosting more than one e-mail domain on a single OS deployment is a bad idea, and generally other services which don't support domain-based virtualization (as HTTP does with the Host: header) would suffer from the fact that multiple instances would have to listen on different ports, which means only one gets to use the default port for that service.
  • With OS virtualization and multiple outside IP addresses routed into that box, the only limit is the total CPU/memory/storage of that box. For this, you need a Hypervisor package on it. The nice thing about that is each virtual instance will share the same Linux kernel for system calls rather than suffer the penalty of a software layer as with VirtualBox.
